To future generations:  

I, Qiu, Liangzhou painter, served brush and ink forty years, devoted to art. 
Now, breath like a thread, life a dying candle, I tear silk to leave this message. 
When Lord Zhang raised the righteous banner, Hexi returned to Tang, thousands rejoiced at Tianshui Market. 
Witnessing peace, I poured my soul into "Merriment at Skybrim". 
Hu dancers twirl in taverns, Han children play in wheat stacks; camel bells echo on the Silk Road, garrison horns blend with flutes. 
A nine-zhang scroll captures an era's vitality in ink. 

Yet! As I painted, beneath the prosperity lurked omens. 
Tibetan riders shadowed Qilian's snow, couriers brought warnings from Shazhou. 
Fearing this painting might become a lost masterpiece, I split it in three... 
If descendants find the fragments, remember two things: 
First, reassemble it like the Guiyi Army reclaiming lost land—every inch of landscape holds blood and tears. 
Second, when complete, burn incense facing east—not for my bones, but for Chang'an's moon! 
Alas! Art may tear, but the Tang spirit cannot split; fragments may hide, but the longing for home cannot be buried. 


July of Year, Qiu Shizi's Final Words
